planting.note: Transplant nursery seedlings into rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in dappled shade in spring, and bring potted specimens indoors over winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Dawairi takes its name from the Arabic word for 'round,' describing the rounded leaf and cherry shape that distinguishes it from Yemen's other ancient coffee landraces still terraced into the steep, rain-fed mountainsides around Haraaz and Bura'a. Grow it exactly as you would any highland Arabica: filtered shade from taller companion trees, steady moisture without waterlogging, and patience, since the first cherries take three to four years to appear. Hand-harvested and typically dried whole in the cherry, Dawairi beans produce the dense, winey, fruit-forward cup that defines traditional Yemen Mocha coffee. As one of the morphologically distinct populations identified in genetic surveys of Yemen's centuries-old coffee gardens, it represents a genetic lineage largely separate from the Bourbon and Typica lines that spread worldwide.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Transplant seedlings in spring into fertile, well-drained acidic soil under partial shade; grow in a large container and overwinter indoors outside zones 10-11.

directions: Tuffahi means 'apple-like' in Arabic, a nod to the bright, apple-forward aroma and acidity this Yemeni highland landrace is prized for among specialty roasters tracing Mocha coffee back to its terraced origins. Cultivation follows the same pattern as other Arabica coffees: dappled light under taller shade trees, consistently moist but never soggy soil, and a long wait of three to four years before the first harvest of cherries. Traditionally grown on ancient stone terraces at elevation in Yemen's western highlands and naturally processed by sun-drying the whole cherry, Tuffahi contributes some of the fruit-driven character found in classic Yemeni coffee blends. Genetic studies of Yemen's old-growth coffee gardens treat it as one of several named landraces distinct from the globally dispersed Typica and Bourbon lineages.

planting.note: Set out nursery-grown seedlings in spring in rich, acidic, well-draining soil under partial shade; keep as a container plant brought indoors for winter outside zones 10-11.

directions: Udaini is one of the smaller-cherried coffee landraces still cultivated on Yemen's ancient high-elevation terraces, where generations of growers have kept it distinct from the Bourbon and Typica types that later spread across the colonial coffee world. It needs the same basic care as any Arabica: filtered shade, even moisture, acidic well-drained soil, and three to four years of patient growth before the first cherry harvest. Grown without irrigation on rocky mountainside terraces and dried whole in the cherry, Udaini contributes to the complex, winey, fruit-forward profile that specialty roasters seek out in true Yemen Mocha lots. Its persistence as a named, morphologically distinct population makes it a living link to the earliest documented coffee cultivation in the Horn of Africa and Arabian Peninsula.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Start from fresh seed and transplant the young tree into deep, fertile, moisture-retentive tropical soil in full sun once established.

directions: Jengkol is a large nitrogen-fixing legume tree grown throughout West Java and the Betawi region of Indonesia for its flat, dark-brown seeds, which are boiled or fried and served in dishes like semur jengkol and rendang jengkol despite their famously strong, sulfurous aroma similar to but more pungent than the related petai bean. Grow it from fresh seed in deep, well-watered tropical soil in full sun, giving it room to become a substantial shade tree, since it needs several years of growth before the long, curling seed pods begin forming. Harvest pods once they mature and dry slightly on the tree, then soak or parboil the seeds to mellow their odor and bitterness before cooking. The tree is a dooryard and smallholder staple across Indonesia and Malaysia, valued as much for soil-building nitrogen fixation as for its distinctive, polarizing seeds.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Transplant a rooted cutting or young nursery tree in spring into moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and grow in a large container where winters are cool.

directions: Daun salam is the whole, leathery leaf of an evergreen Syzygium tree native to Indonesia and Malaysia, dropped into soups, stews, and simmered dishes like soto and gulai for a subtle, tea-like aromatic depth entirely different from Mediterranean bay laurel, then fished out before serving. Grow it as a slow but steady tree in full sun to partial shade with consistently moist, fertile soil, propagating most reliably from rooted cuttings or air-layers since seed-grown trees are slower and less uniform. Established trees tolerate occasional pruning well, which keeps container-grown specimens at a manageable size for leaf picking in cooler climates where the tree must be moved indoors for winter. Fresh or dried leaves are picked year-round once the tree is a couple of years old, making it a long-term pantry staple in home gardens across the Indonesian archipelago.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens Plants of the World Online
Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plant Products

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out only after nights stay reliably warm, since this highland landrace resents cold, wet soil.

directions: Katokkon is a squat, deeply wrinkled, bell-shaped pepper grown by the Toraja people of the South Sulawesi highlands in Indonesia, where its habanero-level heat and fruity aroma make it the signature chili in smoky pa'piong dishes and fiery sambal. Despite its tropical origin at cooler mountain elevations, it grows in a home garden much like a habanero or other Capsicum chinense type: start seed indoors in a warm spot, transplant after the soil has thoroughly warmed, and give plants full sun with steady but not excessive moisture. The thick-walled, globe-shaped pods ripen from green to orange-red and are typically picked and used fresh or dried for sambal paste rather than pickled. It is recognized by Slow Food's Ark of Taste as a distinct Toraja heirloom variety worth preserving against the spread of generic commercial chili seed.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity Ark of Taste
Indonesian Ministry of Agriculture Plant Variety Protection records
